verdict.reason: Both debates move from the Gulf Stream slogan to an ocean-plus-wind partnership, but B keeps building the mechanism further (stored seasonal heat versus resupply, the west-coast/east-coast asymmetry, the Rockies bending the westerlies), and each objection narrows a claim. A reaches the battery/delivery-truck point by Turn 4, then spends its last turns guessing why the user is asking. B's closing map gives observable tests that would separate the explanations, which is what this exploratory question needs.

comparisons.a_observation: After the good concession in Turn 4 and the narrowed conveyor claim in Turn 7, the Wind Mechanic stops arguing the mechanism. He speculates about the asker's motives (school story, weighing a move) and ranks them, and Turn 10 only disputes that ranking.
comparisons.b_observation: The Conveyor Skeptic concedes stored summer heat and narrows his claim, but points out that the reservoir drains by midwinter without resupply. Turns 7-8 then add the continental-geometry and Rockies wave argument, and Turns 10-11 settle on an explicit division of credit with the proportion still open.
comparisons.why_it_matters: The user wants to know why the gap exists. B's ending knows more than its opening on several separate mechanisms, while A's second half drifts away from the mechanism.

comparisons.aspect: Usefulness for exploration (what would settle it)
comparisons.a_observation: It separates coastal from inland comparisons and suggests reading published estimates of ocean versus atmospheric heat transport. That is reasonable, but it points to a reading rather than a test.
comparisons.b_observation: It gives three tests, each tied to one explanation: whether the same west-warm/east-cold pattern shows up on other continents, whether past circulation slowdowns cooled Europe specifically, and whether the contrast is much larger in winter than in summer at matched coastal and inland stations.
comparisons.why_it_matters: For an exploratory question, naming the evidence that separates competing explanations is the most useful output, and B's tests can actually be checked.

comparisons.a_observation: It turns the question toward the asker's purpose and the pattern's durability, a personal framing the user never raised.
comparisons.b_observation: It stays on the mechanism and the disputed proportions. Its self-reflection line is light and about the explanation itself.
comparisons.why_it_matters: The brief warns against forcing a personal dilemma onto an explanatory question. A does this, at a small cost.

verdict.best_of_a: A.debate[7].text: It names the user's unstated fact, which places are being compared, and shows how coastal Labrador versus inland Ontario changes whose explanation carries the most weight.
verdict.best_of_b: B.debate[7].text: The Rockies stationary-wave argument adds a separate atmospheric mechanism that explains why cold air floods eastern North America. It turns the debate from ocean versus wind into a three-part account.

concerns.description: The Pacific coast of Canada and Alaska is offered as a case with no large current involved, but the North Pacific and Alaska Currents do run there, so the test is less clean than stated.
'No ocean current is needed to explain it' overstates the case. Turn 11 later softens it to a joint product, but the line is stated with more certainty than the evidence supports.

The view that the atmosphere moves most of the heat and the popular story overrates the current is attributed to Stommel's Gulf Stream book, which is mainly about the current's dynamics. The attribution may blur the book's idea with the mind's own extension.
